title: Linear scans & complexity
description: Use a loop invariant to justify a one-pass maximum search and explain its time and space cost.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.body: An algorithm is a precise procedure with a contract: valid inputs, expected outputs, and the conditions under which it works. Complexity describes how work and storage grow as input grows. A linear scan is O(n); repeatedly halving a search interval is O(log n). Big O is an upper bound, not a measurement in milliseconds. Explain the invariant that stays true as your algorithm runs before choosing an optimization.

sections.title: Work through an example
sections.body: Imagine finding the maximum in [4, 2, 9, 1]. Keep the largest value seen so far. After each element, the candidate is the maximum of the processed prefix. That invariant proves the result after the final element. You inspect every item once and keep one candidate: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. An empty collection needs an explicit contract; this exercise returns null.

sections.title: Engineering judgement
sections.body: Nested loops do not always mean quadratic work: an inner pointer that only moves forward may visit n positions in total. Distinguish worst-case, average-case, and amortized cost. Compare actual timings only after checking correctness on empty, duplicate, and negative inputs. The engineering goal is a clear argument plus evidence, not just an impressive complexity label.

question: Implement maxValue(nums). Return the maximum numeric value, or null for an empty array. Use one pass and constant extra space. Explain your invariant in your notes.

video.note: Watch the discussion of correctness and running time, then apply both ideas to the maximum scan. The exercise is a small linear-time example of the same analysis.

title: Frequency maps & unique characters
description: Count character frequencies with a map, then find the first character whose count is one.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.body: A map associates keys with values. A set records membership. Hash tables aim for expected constant-time lookup, insert, and delete under suitable hashing and load-factor assumptions. Collisions still need resolution. Frequency counting transforms repeated searches into a single scan: update the count for each item, then inspect the resulting counts.

sections.title: Work through an example
sections.body: To find the first unique character in swiss, count every character: s appears three times, w once, and i once. A second scan in the original order finds w first. Returning the first key in some arbitrary map order would not express the real requirement. Two O(n) passes still give O(n) total time, with O(k) storage for k distinct characters.

sections.title: Engineering judgement
sections.body: Use Map rather than a plain object for unconstrained keys; object prototypes can make names such as constructor surprising. Unicode needs an explicit unit: JavaScript string indexing uses UTF-16 code units, while for...of iterates code points. This exercise returns a character, avoiding an index-unit mismatch. Human-perceived graphemes can require further segmentation.

question: Implement firstUnique(text). Return the first code point that occurs once, or null if none exists. Preserve original order.

title: Stacks & balanced brackets
description: Use a last-in, first-out stack to validate matching and correctly nested brackets.

sections.title: The stack contract
sections.body: A stack is last-in, first-out: the newest unfinished item is the next one processed. Nested brackets have precisely this structure. In a string such as ([{}]), the opening brace is the first opening symbol that must be closed. Keep a stack of unmatched opening brackets. The contract after every character is that this stack contains exactly the still-open brackets, in their opening order.

sections.title: Match the most recent opening
sections.body: When reading an opening bracket, push it. When reading a closing bracket, compare it with the most recent opening bracket and pop only if the pair matches. For ([)], the closing parenthesis encounters an opening square bracket, so the string is invalid even though the total counts might balance. At the end, an empty stack means every opening bracket was closed.

sections.title: Choose and test the boundaries
sections.body: Each bracket is pushed or popped at most once, giving O(n) time and O(n) worst-case auxiliary space for n characters. This exercise ignores non-bracket text, whereas the video problem contains only bracket symbols. Check an empty string, an unmatched closing symbol, an unclosed opening symbol, adjacent pairs, and incorrectly nested pairs. Counting openings and closings alone cannot prove correct nesting.

question: Implement balanced(text) for (), [], and {}. Ignore all other characters. Return true only when nesting and ordering are valid.

title: Sorted arrays & two pointers
description: Use sorted order to move two pointers safely while searching for a target pair sum.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.body: An array stores an ordered sequence. Indexing is constant time in the conventional RAM model; inserting near the beginning shifts later items. A dynamic array occasionally allocates a larger buffer, so append is usually amortized constant time. Two pointers let you reason about a pair of positions while avoiding an exhaustive comparison of every pair.

sections.title: Work through an example
sections.body: For sorted input [1, 3, 4, 7] and target 8, start at the ends: 1 + 7 = 8. If the sum were smaller, moving the right pointer left could only make it smaller, so move the left pointer right. If larger, move the right pointer left. Each move rules out a row or column of impossible pairs. At most n pointer movements are needed.

sections.title: Engineering judgement
sections.body: The sorted-input precondition is essential. Sorting an unsorted input costs O(n log n) and changes positions; preserve original indices when the output needs them. Define whether you return one pair or every pair. Avoid using the same element twice. Test duplicate values and inputs with fewer than two elements.

question: Implement pairSum(sorted, target). Return the two indices of the first match reached by the end-to-end two-pointer algorithm, or null. The array is sorted ascending.

title: Binary search & insertion boundaries
description: Maintain a half-open interval to find the first value at least as large as a target.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.body: Binary search needs a monotonic predicate: false before a boundary and true from the boundary onward. It is more general than finding one exact value in a sorted array. Examples include the first feasible capacity, the first failing version, or a lower bound. The main challenge is maintaining an interval convention consistently.

sections.title: Work through an example
sections.body: For lowerBound([2, 4, 4, 9], 4), keep a half-open interval [lo, hi). If nums[mid] is below the target, every index up to mid is too small, so set lo = mid + 1. Otherwise set hi = mid. On termination lo equals hi and is the first position whose value is at least the target. It may equal the array length.

sections.title: Engineering judgement
sections.body: An exact-match search that returns immediately can return any duplicate, not the leftmost one. Check arrays of length zero and one, targets before the first item and after the last, and repeated items. Explain termination: every update strictly shrinks the search interval. Use arithmetic midpoint calculation rather than bitwise tricks that coerce numbers to 32 bits.

question: Implement lowerBound(nums, target), returning the first index with value >= target, or nums.length if no such position exists.

title: Binary tree depth & recursion
description: Define a recursive subtree contract and compute a binary tree’s maximum depth.

sections.title: A precise recursive contract
sections.body: A binary tree node has at most two children. To calculate maximum depth, define the answer as the number of nodes on the longest path from the current root to a leaf. Give every recursive call that same contract. An absent child has depth zero, and a leaf has depth one. Thinking in terms of the answer for a subtree makes the recursive step small enough to justify.

sections.title: Combine the subtree answers
sections.body: For each node, compute the depth of the left subtree and the right subtree, take the larger result, and add one for the current node. A root with two leaf children therefore has depth two. A chain of three nodes has depth three. You do not need a binary-search-tree ordering rule; the operation depends on the structure, not the stored values.

sections.title: Account for depth and malformed structure
sections.body: Every node is visited once, so the traversal takes O(n) time. Recursive calls use O(h) stack space for tree height h, which can grow to n in a skewed tree. An explicit stack can avoid the language call-stack limit on very deep inputs. The input contract is an acyclic tree; arbitrary cyclic graph data needs a visited set rather than this tree-only recursion.

title: Breadth-first search & shortest paths
description: Explore an unweighted graph in distance layers with a queue and visited set.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.body: A graph represents entities and relationships. An adjacency list stores the neighbors of each vertex and is efficient for sparse graphs. Breadth-first search explores vertices by distance in edges from a source. In an unweighted graph, the first time a vertex is discovered gives its shortest-path distance from that source.

sections.title: Work through an example
sections.body: For A connected to B and C, with B connected to D, start with queue [A] and distance A=0. Discover B and C at distance one, then D at distance two. Mark a node when enqueuing it, not when removing it, so multiple incoming edges do not schedule duplicate work. A parent map can reconstruct the actual route.

sections.title: Engineering judgement
sections.body: BFS gives fewest edges, not minimum total weight when weights differ. Dijkstra needs nonnegative edge weights; negative edges need another method. An adjacency-list BFS takes O(V+E) over the reachable graph. Disconnected nodes remain unreachable. Always test cycles, self-loops, an isolated source, and source equal to target.

title: Dynamic programming & coin change
description: Define minimum-coins subproblems and compute them bottom-up instead of relying on a greedy choice.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.body: Dynamic programming avoids solving the same subproblem repeatedly. Start by stating what one state means, then write its transition, base cases, and evaluation order. Memoization evaluates states on demand; tabulation evaluates them in a planned order. The runtime often follows from the number of states multiplied by the work per transition.

sections.title: Work through an example
sections.body: For the minimum coins needed to make amount a, define dp[a] as that minimum, with dp[0]=0. For each positive coin c no larger than a, consider 1 + dp[a-c]. Taking the minimum gives the recurrence. Compute increasing amounts so every dependency is ready. Infinity represents an impossible subtotal; convert the final impossible result to -1.

sections.title: Engineering judgement
sections.body: A greedy largest-coin strategy fails for denominations [1, 3, 4] and amount 6: 4+1+1 uses three coins while 3+3 uses two. This DP uses O(amount × coins.length) time and O(amount) storage, which is pseudo-polynomial in the numeric amount. This exercise assumes nonnegative integer amounts and positive integer coins.

title: Vectors & cosine similarity
description: Compute a dot product and vector norms, then use cosine similarity to compare directions.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.body: A vector is an ordered list of numbers. In machine learning it can encode measurements, token representations, or learned features. A dot product combines aligned components. A norm measures magnitude. Cosine similarity divides the dot product by both magnitudes, measuring direction rather than scale. It is useful only when the representation makes direction meaningful.

sections.title: Work through an example
sections.body: For a=[1,0] and b=[3,0], the dot product is 3, but cosine similarity is 1 because their directions match. For a=[1,0] and b=[0,2], similarity is 0 because they are perpendicular. Normalizing vectors first makes their dot product equal cosine similarity. A zero vector has no direction; this exercise defines its similarity as zero.

sections.title: Engineering judgement
sections.body: High cosine similarity is evidence of proximity in one embedding space, not proof of factual agreement. Different embedding models generally produce incompatible spaces. Check dimensions, avoid accidental broadcasting, and keep preprocessing consistent. For retrieval, evaluate whether the right document appears near the top rather than assuming a similarity threshold is universal.

question: Implement cosine(a, b). Inputs have equal length and finite numbers. Return 0 if either norm is zero. Results are checked with numeric tolerance.

title: Neurons, weighted sums & ReLU
description: Calculate a neuron’s weighted sum and bias, then apply the ReLU activation.

sections.title: One neuron is a small calculation
sections.body: A dense neuron combines input features with learned weights, adds a bias, and applies an activation. Write the preactivation as z = sum(inputs[i] * weights[i]) + bias. ReLU returns max(0, z). A layer applies several such calculations to the same input. Nonlinear activations let a stack of layers represent more than a single affine transformation.

sections.title: Calculate a forward pass
sections.body: With inputs [2, -1], weights [0.5, 1], and bias 0.2, the weighted terms sum to zero, so z is 0.2 and the ReLU output is 0.2. With input [1], weight [2], and bias -3, z is -1 and ReLU returns zero. Empty input and weight lists leave only the bias; the exercise explicitly tests this boundary.

sections.title: Separate computation from training
sections.body: This lesson implements a forward calculation, not a training algorithm. Inputs and weights must have equal lengths so that each feature has a corresponding weight. Keep that shape contract visible when moving to layers and batches. Once you can explain this forward pass, the later gradient-descent lesson shows how a loss can guide changes to parameters. Do not confuse a larger network with a guarantee of useful predictions.

title: Logits, softmax & numerical stability
description: Convert logits into a probability distribution using a numerically stable softmax.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.body: A classifier often produces real-valued scores called logits. Softmax converts them into nonnegative values that sum to one by exponentiating each logit and dividing by the total. The resulting distribution expresses the model output; it is not automatically a calibrated probability of being correct. Calibration must be checked on representative held-out data.

sections.title: Work through an example
sections.body: For logits [0,0], both exponentials equal one, so softmax returns [0.5,0.5]. For [1000,1000], direct exponentiation overflows. Subtract the largest logit first: exp(x_i-m) / sum(exp(x_j-m)). The shared factor cancels algebraically, preserving the distribution while avoiding large positive exponents.

sections.title: Engineering judgement
sections.body: Changing temperature changes concentration: divide logits by a positive temperature before softmax. Low temperature favors the largest score; higher temperature spreads mass more evenly. Handle empty inputs explicitly and test very large equal logits. Small probabilities can still underflow; computing log probabilities directly with log-sum-exp is preferable in many loss calculations.

question: Implement softmax(logits) with max subtraction. Return [] for an empty array. Do not overflow for inputs around 1000.

title: Gradient descent from scratch
description: Reduce a differentiable loss by updating a parameter opposite its gradient.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.body: Training chooses parameters that reduce an objective. For a differentiable scalar loss L(w), the derivative describes local sensitivity to w. Gradient descent updates w to w minus learning_rate times the derivative. In multiple dimensions the gradient collects all partial derivatives. The learning rate controls how far the update travels, so both its size and the loss geometry matter.

sections.title: Work through an example
sections.body: For L(w)=(w-3)^2, the derivative is 2(w-3). Start at w=0 and use a learning rate of 0.1: the first update gives 0.6 and the second gives 1.08. Each step moves closer to 3. At rate 1, this particular quadratic oscillates between 0 and 6. Larger steps are not automatically faster learning.

sections.title: Engineering judgement
sections.body: Learning curves reveal divergence, stalled optimization, and overfitting, but training loss alone cannot tell whether a model generalizes. Split data before fitting transformations and keep a final test set untouched during tuning. Fix seeds when practical, record hyperparameters, and compare with a simple baseline. This exercise isolates optimization; it is not a complete training pipeline.

title: Confusion matrices & classifier metrics
description: Count classification outcomes and derive precision and recall, including zero-denominator cases.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.body: An evaluation is a repeatable test of behavior against explicit criteria. For classifiers, accuracy measures overall correctness, precision measures how many positive predictions are correct, and recall measures how many actual positives were found. These metrics answer different questions. For generative systems, use task-specific checks, groundedness review, and human assessment rather than one universal score.

sections.title: Work through an example
sections.body: For actual labels [1,1,0,0] and predicted labels [1,0,1,0], there is one true positive, one false positive, and one false negative. Precision and recall are both 0.5. A model that always predicts the majority class can have high accuracy on imbalanced data yet be useless for finding rare events. Always compare with such simple baselines.

sections.title: Engineering judgement
sections.body: Keep evaluation cases versioned and separate from tuning examples. Break failures down by category, input length, and user task. Track latency and cost alongside quality. Small datasets have uncertainty; a tiny average improvement may be noise. For retrieval, inspect recall at k and the quality of cited evidence. For tool-using systems, test incorrect tool arguments and unsafe instruction following.

question: Implement metrics(actual, predicted) for 0/1 labels. Return {precision, recall}. If a denominator is zero, return 0 for that metric. Arrays have equal length.

title: Schema validation for AI tool requests
description: Validate the structure, allowed action, and query bounds of a proposed search-tool request before executing it.

sections.title: Treat a proposed tool call as structured input
sections.body: A model or another external component can propose a structured search request, but a proposed object is still untrusted input. Define an explicit contract before executing it: a supported action, required fields, field types, and bounds. JSON Schema expresses such shape constraints declaratively; a small hand-written predicate can enforce a narrow contract too. Valid structure is one boundary, not permission to perform arbitrary actions.

sections.title: Validate the search request
sections.body: For this lesson, accept a non-array object with action exactly search and a query string whose trimmed length is between one and two hundred characters. Reject null, unsupported actions, missing strings, whitespace-only queries, and excessively long text. The reference video demonstrates writing and applying a JSON schema to structured API data. The exercise applies the same validation method to a proposed search-tool request without requiring an external tool or service.

sections.title: Keep validation separate from execution
sections.body: Return a validation result before calling any tool. A structurally valid request may still need application authorization and an execution budget; schema validation does not establish that a model’s claims are true. Keep unknown actions disabled, avoid treating retrieved text as trusted instructions, and report invalid fields clearly. This lesson focuses on the validation boundary; it does not claim to implement a complete agent, model service, or security policy.

title: Scaled dot-product attention
description: Score query–key pairs, apply stable softmax, and combine values using the resulting weights.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.body: Attention combines value vectors using weights determined by a query and a set of keys. Scaled dot-product attention computes scores q·k/sqrt(d), normalizes them with softmax, and takes a weighted sum of values. Keys answer where to look; values provide the information to combine. A transformer uses learned projections and multiple heads to do this in parallel.

sections.title: Work through an example
sections.body: If a query scores two keys equally, their values receive equal weight. With scalar values 2 and 6, the output is 4. If one score is much larger, the result moves toward that key's value. In causal language modeling, a mask prevents a position from attending to future tokens. Position information is also needed to represent order.

sections.title: Engineering judgement
sections.body: Check tensor axes carefully: normalizing over features instead of key positions changes the operation. Standard full self-attention constructs a quadratic-size score matrix in sequence length, although implementations can reduce memory overhead. Attention weights are not a complete causal explanation of a model. This exercise handles one query and scalar values to expose the core mechanics.

question: Implement attend(query, keys, values). Compute scaled dot-product scores, stable softmax, then a weighted sum of scalar values. Return 0 for no keys. Query dimension is positive.

title: Retrieval for grounded answers
description: Retrieve relevant evidence for a question and evaluate the retrieval stage before generating an answer.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.body: Retrieval-augmented generation separates finding evidence from generating an answer. A typical pipeline parses documents, chunks text, creates an index, retrieves candidate chunks, optionally reranks them, and supplies evidence to a generator. Chunk boundaries and metadata influence whether a retrieved passage can support a useful answer.

sections.title: Work through an example
sections.body: A minimal baseline can rank documents by overlap with a query. For query cache latency, a passage containing both terms should rank above an unrelated passage. Dense embeddings help with semantic matches, while lexical retrieval often handles exact identifiers well. Start with a baseline you can inspect, then measure whether a more complex retriever improves recall.

sections.title: Engineering judgement
sections.body: Keep source IDs and document versions with every chunk so answers can cite evidence. Retrieved text is untrusted data, not instructions. Handle questions for which the corpus has no answer, and evaluate retrieval separately from generation. This playground implements a lexical ranking baseline only; it does not call a language model or pretend to generate grounded answers.

title: Accessible names & form labels
description: Give interactive controls meaningful accessible names using native labels and appropriate ARIA overrides.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.body: Interactive HTML controls need meaningful accessible names. A native label connected to an input supplies a programmatic name; aria-label can provide an explicit name where appropriate. A placeholder is a hint, not a stable substitute for a label. Prefer native controls so keyboard behavior and semantics come with the element. This lesson focuses on how controls are named, rather than a general tour of all accessibility techniques.

sections.title: Work through an example
sections.body: For a search input, a label such as Search lessons tells assistive technology what the control is for. In the simplified exercise, a nonempty ariaLabel takes precedence over label, and a blank override falls back to the label. Trim both strings. If neither supplies a name, return null. Real browser name computation also handles aria-labelledby, native text, hidden content, and other rules; this challenge deliberately models only its stated subset.

sections.title: Engineering judgement
sections.body: Check controls that have a native label, an explicit ARIA name, an empty ARIA override, and only a placeholder. Keep visible wording and programmatic names consistent so people using voice input can refer to the text they see. The video demonstrates labels and accessible names on real controls; the exercise makes the naming precedence explicit. Try a native label/input pair in the HTML/CSS playground after completing the predicate.

question: Implement accessibleName(control). This simplified exercise accepts {label, ariaLabel, placeholder}. Return the trimmed nonempty ariaLabel first, otherwise label, otherwise null. A placeholder is not accepted as a label.

video.title: The art of labeling -- A11ycasts #12
video.creator: Chrome for Developers
video.note: Follow how controls receive accessible names and why placeholders are insufficient. Our exercise models only the label and aria-label subset; it is not the complete browser accessible-name algorithm.

title: Responsive grids & column sizing
description: Fit minimum-width cards into a responsive grid while accounting for the gaps between columns.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.body: CSS layout is a constraint system. Normal flow provides the default document order; Flexbox distributes items along a primary axis; Grid defines rows and columns together. The box model includes content, padding, border, and margin. Using border-box makes declared width include padding and border, which makes component sizing easier to reason about.

sections.title: Work through an example
sections.body: For a card grid, compute how many minimum-width cards fit after accounting for gaps. Three 240px cards and two 24px gaps need 768px. With 700px of space, only two fit. CSS can express this directly with repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 240px), 1fr)), letting the browser choose columns while avoiding overflow on narrower screens.

sections.title: Engineering judgement
sections.body: Design breakpoints around content pressure, not a list of device brands. Avoid fixed heights for text containers and give grid children min-width:0 when long content can overflow. Test zoom, long labels, keyboard focus, and reduced motion. Layout shift can be reduced by reserving space for media. Use the HTML/CSS mode to build and resize a responsive card.

question: Implement columns(width, minimum, gap). Return the number of minimum-width columns that fit, with gaps only between columns, and at least 1. Width and gap are nonnegative; minimum is positive.

video.note: Focus on making the grid dynamic with auto-fit and fixing narrow-screen behavior. The exercise computes the same column-capacity constraint before you try a visual version in the HTML/CSS playground.

title: JavaScript arrays & immutable updates
description: Transform an array into a new array and replace the changed object without mutating the original state.

sections.title: Transform values without changing the input
sections.body: An array is an ordered collection, and map builds a new array by applying a callback to each element. An array of objects contains references to those objects. Creating a new outer array does not by itself clone each object. An immutable update therefore replaces the changed object and the outer array while leaving the original values untouched.

sections.title: Update exactly one todo
sections.body: Given [{id: 1, done: false}, {id: 2, done: true}], mapping over the list lets you return {...todo, done: !todo.done} only for the matching ID. Return each other item unchanged. The new list represents the next state. The original list must still contain the original done values. The exercise checks value behavior and runs the function against frozen inputs to expose mutation.

sections.title: Know what a shallow copy guarantees
sections.body: The spread operator makes a shallow object copy: nested objects inside it are still shared unless you replace them too. Copy along the path of the change rather than using JSON serialization as a universal clone. An unknown ID should yield an equivalent new list, and an empty list should remain empty. This array-transformation skill is used by the later pure-function and derived-React-state lessons.

question: Implement toggleTodo(todos, id). Return a new array with a new object for the matching todo and its done value inverted. Other values should be preserved. Do not mutate the input.

title: Pure functions & testable UI logic
description: Keep a UI calculation pure so it can be checked with repeatable input/output tests.

sections.title: Keep a calculation pure
sections.body: A pure function returns the same result for the same input and does not change state outside itself. It does not read the clock, write storage, manipulate the DOM, or mutate its arguments. Moving a UI calculation into such a function makes the contract visible. Rendering and persistence can then use the result without being mixed into the arithmetic.

sections.title: Derive a progress percentage
sections.body: For a progress record, count the read, watched, and practised flags that are truthy. Divide the count by three, multiply by one hundred, and round. One completed activity gives 33; two give 67; all three give 100. Missing progress gives zero. The exercise implements this calculation independently of any framework, storage service, or screen.

sections.title: Test observable behavior and preserve the input
sections.body: Repeatable input/output checks are a natural fit for pure functions. Test missing input, an empty record, partial completion, and full completion. Keep the original record unchanged after the call. The browser can store the source progress record and derive the percentage when displaying it, rather than saving a second percentage value that could become inconsistent. Later lessons reuse this separation for React filtering and async state updates.

question: Implement completion(progress), returning a rounded percentage of truthy read, watched, and practised flags. A missing progress object counts as no completed activities.

video.creator: Web Dev Simplified
video.note: Identify deterministic output and the absence of side effects. Our progress-percentage function is an example of the same pure calculation, tested with partial, complete, and missing input.

title: Async requests & stale responses
description: Prevent an obsolete asynchronous request from overwriting the result of a newer request.

sections.title: Requests can finish out of order
sections.body: An asynchronous operation can complete after a newer operation has started. A search for re may take longer than the following search for react. If the older response is allowed to update the interface last, it overwrites the newer results. Treat the right to commit a result as a separate decision from whether a request happened to finish successfully.

sections.title: Give each request an identity
sections.body: Increase a request ID whenever a new search begins. Capture that ID when starting the request, and compare it with the current latest ID before committing the response. Only an equal pair may update the UI. The playground implements this exact commit boundary. It also rejects a response with an unknown future ID instead of assuming that a larger ID is automatically valid.

sections.title: Cancel obsolete work and still guard the commit
sections.body: AbortController lets a request receive a cancellation signal. The selected video chapter shows that cancellation mechanism. A request-ID guard is complementary: cancellation can arrive after work has completed, and some operations are not cancellable. Model loading, empty, success, and error states explicitly; treat cancellation as an expected outcome. Keep the guard even when you also cancel obsolete network work.

question: Implement shouldCommit(latestId, responseId). Return true only when the response belongs to the current request. This tiny guard is the state-commit boundary; add a race-condition explanation in your notes.

video.title: I Cannot Believe Abort Controller Can Do This
video.creator: Web Dev Simplified
video.note: The selected chapter shows cancelling obsolete work with AbortController. The exercise practices the complementary commit guard: accept a result only when its request ID is current.

title: Runtime type guards & validation
description: Check unknown input at runtime before treating it as a typed user object.

sections.title: Runtime data starts as unknown
sections.body: A TypeScript annotation describes an expected shape during development, but it does not validate JSON arriving at runtime. A type assertion does not check the value. A type guard performs actual checks before the program relies on a narrower type. For a user record, begin by checking for a non-null object and excluding arrays, then validate each required property.

sections.title: Check the user contract
sections.body: The exercise accepts a positive integer id and a name string whose trimmed length is nonzero. Values such as {id: "1", name: "Ada"}, null, and {id: 1, name: " "} must fail. Extra properties are allowed by this particular contract. The function returns a boolean; in TypeScript, the same checked boundary can be wrapped with a predicate return type such as value is User.

sections.title: Validate before using or storing the value
sections.body: Narrowing is useful only after the runtime checks are accurate. Avoid using any or an unchecked type assertion to make an uncertain external value appear safe. Decide whether extra fields are allowed, how empty strings are treated, and which numeric bounds apply. This playground executes the JavaScript validation logic; the video shows how that logic participates in TypeScript narrowing. Both activities are about the same user-shape boundary.

question: Implement isUser(value). Accept a non-array object with an integer id > 0 and a nonempty trimmed string name. Extra properties are allowed.

video.note: Follow how a type guard checks values before narrowing a type. Our JavaScript challenge implements the runtime checks that a TypeScript user-defined type guard would wrap.

title: React state & derived product filters
description: Store minimal React state and derive visible products from the query and stock toggle.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.body: A React component is a function that describes UI. Props supply data from its parent, and useState stores values changed by interaction. For a filterable list, state can hold a query string and an onlyStocked flag, while products arrive as props. A setter schedules a new render. Compute visible products from those inputs instead of storing a second filtered list that must be synchronized.

sections.title: Work through an example
sections.body: For a filterable product list, store the query and the in-stock toggle. Derive the visible products from the original list. Do not separately store the filtered list and its count. When a user edits a product, the derived list updates from one source of truth. Use stable product IDs as keys so identity survives reordering.

sections.title: Engineering judgement
sections.body: Keep the visible-products calculation pure: the same products, query, and stock flag should give the same result without changing any product. Derive the list during rendering, and derive its count from its length. An effect is unnecessary just to mirror a filter result into another state variable. The video identifies that duplicate-state mistake, and the playground implements the filtering calculation that avoids it. Test an empty query, a case-insensitive match, unstocked products, and an empty list.

question: Implement visibleProducts(products, query, onlyStocked). Match name case-insensitively using includes, and filter unstocked products only when onlyStocked is true. Preserve order.

title: LRU caches for frontend data
description: Keep a bounded data cache and evict the least recently used entry after each access.

sections.title: A bounded cache needs an eviction policy
sections.body: A frontend can reuse data already loaded for a key, but an unbounded cache keeps growing. Least recently used eviction removes the entry that has gone longest without being accessed. Every hit refreshes recency, as does inserting a new key. The cache must maintain both membership and the order of use; a set of keys alone does not capture the policy.

sections.title: Trace the same access sequence
sections.body: With capacity two and accesses [a, b, a, c], the order after the first two accesses is [a, b]. Accessing a moves it to the most-recent end, producing [b, a]. Inserting c exceeds capacity, so b is evicted and the order becomes [a, c]. The exercise returns keys from least recently used to most recently used after every access has been processed.

sections.title: Separate recency from freshness
sections.body: A JavaScript Map preserves insertion order, so removing and reinserting a key can model recency for this exercise. In the linked implementation, a hash map and doubly linked list make the same ordering explicit. Capacity zero retains no entries. A production data cache also needs freshness rules, appropriate cache keys, and limits for sensitive data; LRU alone does not decide when a cached answer is still valid.

question: Implement cacheKeys(capacity, accesses), simulating an LRU cache. Each access inserts or refreshes the key. Return keys from least to most recently used. Capacity is a nonnegative integer.
